note.explanation: IPv4 uses 32 bits, so it has 2³² = 4,294,967,296 possible addresses. IPv6 uses 128 bits and was designed to provide many more addresses as the number of internet-connected devices grew. The textbook’s IPv4 example, 172.16.254.1, has four decimal parts, each corresponding to an 8-bit binary group.
examples: IPv6: 2001:0000:130F:0000:0000:0900:876A:130B is an example of an IPv6 address.
note.simple: IPv4 is like a set of 4.3 billion address labels. IPv6 uses far more bits, so it can provide vastly more labels for connected devices.
note.checkQuestion: How many bits does an IPv6 address use?
note.title: IPv4 and IPv6 address sizes
steps: Count the bits in an IPv4 address: 32.
An IPv4 address is written as four decimal numbers, each from 0 to 255.
Count the bits in an IPv6 address: 128.
Remember that IPv6 was designed to address the depletion of IPv4 addresses.
note.answer: IPv4 uses 32 bits; IPv6 uses 128 bits.

mcqs.stem: How many bits are used in an IPv4 address scheme?
rationales: Correct: IPv4 uses a 32-bit address scheme.
Incorrect: IPv4 addresses are not 16 bits long.
Incorrect: 64 bits is not the IPv4 address size given in the section.
Incorrect: 128 bits is the size of an IPv6 address.

mcqs.stem: Which calculation gives the total number of possible IPv4 addresses?
rationales: Correct: 32 bits have 2³² possible combinations.
Incorrect: 2¹⁶ represents combinations of 16 bits, not 32.
Incorrect: 2⁶⁴ represents combinations of 64 bits.
Incorrect: 2¹²⁸ is the number of combinations for 128 bits.

mcqs.stem: How many unique addresses are possible in IPv4?
rationales: Correct: 2³² equals 4,294,967,296.
Incorrect: This is not the total number of IPv4 combinations.
Incorrect: This is not the total number of IPv4 combinations.
Incorrect: This is far less than 2³².

mcqs.stem: How are IPv4 addresses written according to the section?
rationales: Correct: An IPv4 address is written in four sets of decimal numbers from 0 to 255.
Incorrect: IPv4 is not written as two decimal numbers.
Incorrect: The section specifies four sets, not eight.
Incorrect: Each number must be from 0 to 255, not 0 to 999.

mcqs.stem: What is the size of the IPv6 address scheme?
rationales: Correct: IPv6 uses a 128-bit address scheme.
Incorrect: 32 bits is the IPv4 address size.
Incorrect: 8 bits is the size of one IPv4 group, not an IPv6 address.
Incorrect: The section gives 128 bits, not 256.

options: To provide many more unique addresses as internet use grows
To make every IPv4 address shorter
To convert all addresses into decimal numbers
rationales: Correct: IPv6 was developed to address IPv4 address depletion as internet use and connected devices grew.
Incorrect: The section does not say IPv6 was made to shorten IPv4 addresses.
Incorrect: IPv6 is an Internet Protocol version, not a replacement for computer networks.

IPv4 uses more bits than IPv6
mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly compares the IPv4 and IPv6 address sizes?
rationales: Correct: IPv6 uses 128 bits, while IPv4 uses 32 bits.
Incorrect: The bit sizes are the other way around.
Incorrect: IPv6 does not use 32 bits.

mcqs.stem: Which kind of address is a unique identifier assigned to a device connected to the Internet?
rationales: Incorrect: IPv4 addresses are IP identifiers, but the definition applies to IP addresses generally.
Incorrect: IPv6 addresses are IP identifiers, but the definition applies to IP addresses generally.
Correct: Both IPv4 and IPv6 are versions of IP addresses that identify connected devices.
Incorrect: The section identifies IP addresses as unique identifiers for connected devices.

written.text:
Q6.9. An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number. Calculate the total number of unique IPv4 addresses possible.
(a) Show the calculation for the total number of IPv4 addresses.
(b) How many addresses are left if 10% of the total addresses are reserved for special purposes?
written.finalAnswer: (a) 2³² = 4,294,967,296 unique addresses. (b) 90% of 4,294,967,296 = 3,865,470,566.4, or approximately 3,865,470,566 whole addresses.

rubric.why: The calculation must show that all combinations of 32 bits are counted.
rubric.description: Set up the total-address calculation using the 32-bit length.
rubric.how: Write 2³² for the possible combinations of 32 bits.

rubric.why: The evaluated total is needed for the remaining calculation.
rubric.how: Give 4,294,967,296 as the total number of IPv4 addresses.

rubric.why: Finding the reserved portion shows how the remaining number is determined.
rubric.description: Calculate 10% of the total addresses reserved for special purposes.

rubric.why: The final result answers how many addresses remain after reserving 10%.
rubric.description: State the number of addresses left.
rubric.how: Subtract the reserved 10%, or calculate 90% of the total, to get 3,865,470,566.4 (approximately 3,865,470,566 whole addresses).

modelAnswer: Total number of unique IPv4 addresses = 2³²

examTips: This topic can be tested with a short definition or comparison question about IPv4 and IPv6, or a long numerical question using the 32-bit IPv4 address size.
For a calculation, show 2³² before writing 4,294,967,296; the formula and the evaluated answer can earn separate marks.
For a reserved-address part, show the percentage calculation and then state the number left.
Remember the key comparison: IPv4 uses 32 bits; IPv6 uses 128 bits.

hints: The IPv4 address is 32 bits long.
Each bit can be 0 or 1, so use 2³² for all possible combinations.

explain.title: Internet Protocol addresses identify devices
explain.body: Internet Protocol (IP) addresses are unique identifiers assigned to devices connected to the Internet. The two primary versions are IPv4 and IPv6.

explain.title: IPv4 uses 32 bits
explain.body: IPv4 is the fourth version of the Internet Protocol and the most widely used today. It uses a 32-bit address scheme, allowing for approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses. The total is 2³² = 4,294,967,296. IPv4 addresses are written in four sets of decimal numbers, each ranging from 0 to 255.

explain.title: IPv6 uses 128 bits
explain.body: IPv6 is the most recent version of the Internet Protocol designed to replace IPv4. It uses a 128-bit address scheme, allowing for an almost limitless number of unique addresses. It was developed to address the depletion of IPv4 addresses as the internet and connected devices grew.

mistakes: Writing 32 as the total number of IPv4 addresses instead of calculating 2³².
Confusing the 32-bit IPv4 address size with the 128-bit IPv6 address size.
Forgetting that an IPv4 address has four decimal groups, each from 0 to 255.
Calculating the 10% reserved but forgetting to subtract it from the total to find the addresses left.
Leaving out the working in a numerical answer when the question asks to show the calculation.
